content.title: About
content.content: Cobbler is a small berry crop native to temperate regions of North America. Cobbler berries have a sweet‑tart flavor, an aroma reminiscent of raspberry and blueberry, and a juicy flesh with a slightly crisp skin. They are eaten fresh and also used in baking, jams, juices, and desserts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cobbler belongs to the Rosaceae family and is closely related to raspberries and currants.
The berries are rich in anthocyanins, which give them their deep red color.
Cobbler plants can thrive with a short growing season, making them popular among growers in northern latitudes.
Traditionally, indigenous peoples used cobbler berries to make medicinal tinctures.
Cobbler seeds contain a small amount of oil that is used in cosmetic products.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Cobbler berries contain vitamin C and polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports immunity
items.content: Vitamin C and flavonoids contribute to a stronger immune system.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Cobbler berries have a low energy density, making them a good choice for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and maintain normal blood pressure.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic responses to cobbler berries, such as skin rashes or swelling.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: The berries contain oxalates, so people prone to kidney stones should limit consumption.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Commercially grown berries may be treated with pesticides; it is advisable to wash them thoroughly before eating.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cobbler berries can be eaten fresh, added to smoothies, yogurts, and muesli, and are also great in baked goods—pies, muffins, and jams. For sauces, gently mash the berries and mix with a little sugar or honey.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cobbler berries in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a single layer on a tray, then transfer to a bag—this preserves flavor and nutrients for up to 6 months.

cookie-butter-or-sugar-with-icing-or-fil.title: Cookie, butter or sugar, with icing or non‑chocolate filling

content.title: About
content.content: This is a cookie made from a butter‑ or sugar‑based dough, topped with icing or filled with a non‑chocolate filling. Common icings are vanilla, fruit or caramel, while fillings may include jam, cream, nuts or marmalade.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The tradition of icing cookies began in Europe in the 19th century.
In the United States, “Sugar Cookies” with a sweet glaze are a popular holiday treat, often decorated with colored sprinkles.
Fruit fillings such as strawberry or lemon jam are frequently used in festive assortments.
A glaze made from powdered sugar and egg white hardens quickly, creating a crisp surface.
In some regions these are called “shortbread” because of their crumbly texture.

items.title: Quick source of energy
items.content: Sugar and fats in the dough provide rapid glucose and energy for the body.

items.title: Contains small amounts of B‑vitamins
items.content: Flour and eggs supply thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2) and niacin.

items.title: Calcium from dairy ingredients
items.content: When milk or butter is used, the cookie contributes a modest amount of calcium.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of dental caries.

items.title: Gluten and dairy allergies
items.content: Traditional recipes contain wheat flour and dairy, which may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Possible trans‑fat content
items.content: Using margarine instead of butter can introduce trans fats, which are detrimental to heart health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cookies are convenient as a standalone snack, served with tea, or used in dessert platters. They can be further decorated with sprinkles, nuts or dried fruit.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container at room temperature, away from direct sunlight. For longer storage, refrigerate to prevent the icing from softening.

lettuce-salad-with-cheese-tomato-and-or-.title: Lettuce Salad with Cheese, Tomato and/or Carrot, No Dressing

content.title: About
content.content: Lettuce salad is a mix of fresh leafy lettuce, cheese, tomato and carrot, with optional additional vegetables. No dressing is used to preserve the natural flavors of the ingredients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Leafy lettuce is high in water content and helps maintain hydration.
Cheese can be soft (feta, mozzarella) or hard (cheddar, parmesan).
Tomatoes contain lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that is enhanced by cooking but remains beneficial raw.
Carrot is one of the most accessible sources of beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
The absence of dressing makes the salad low‑calorie and allows better control of fat intake.

items.title: Vision support
items.content: Beta‑carotene from carrot and vitamin A help maintain healthy eyesight.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomato and vitamin C from lettuce combat free radicals.

items.title: Bone health
items.content: Calcium from cheese and vitamin K from lettuce contribute to bone strength.

items.title: Hydration and low calories
items.content: High water content and no dressing make the dish light and supportive of fluid balance.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Lettuce and carrot provide fiber that supports digestive regularity.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Non‑organic vegetables may carry pesticide residues; thorough washing is recommended.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: High‑salt cheeses can increase sodium intake; choose low‑salt or reduced‑fat options.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad immediately after chopping to keep it crisp. Optional additions include nuts, seeds, or fresh herbs. A light squeeze of lemon juice can be added if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ingredients separately in the refrigerator: lettuce in an airtight container with a paper towel, cheese wrapped in film, and cut vegetables in a sealed dish. Assembled salad is best consumed within 2‑3 hours.

summer-squash-yellow-or-green-ns-as-to-f.title: Summer squash, yellow or green, NS (cooked)

content.title: About
content.content: Summer squash (Cucurbita pepo) in yellow or green varieties, processed by the NS (natural) method, is ready to eat after cooking. The vegetable has a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a tender yet firm texture. It is used in salads, side dishes, soups, and casseroles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Summer squash belongs to the cucurbit family and is known for rapid growth and high yields.
Yellow and green types differ only in skin color; their taste is virtually identical.
The squash is rich in carotenoids, which give the bright color and act as antioxidants.
The NS process minimizes the use of chemical preservatives, preserving natural flavor and nutrients.
In some cuisines, summer squash is a key ingredient in traditional dishes such as Italian caponata.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Contains beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A, supporting vision and immune function.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Its low energy density makes it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C provides antioxidant protection and is essential for collagen synthesis.

items.title: Minerals: potassium and magnesium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain fluid balance, while magnesium supports muscle function.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to squash.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: If the NS method is not properly applied, pesticide residues may remain; thorough washing is recommended.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large portions can cause gas due to the fiber content.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Squash can be eaten raw in salads, roasted, sautéed, added to soups, or stir‑fried. Typically it is cut into cubes or slices before cooking. It works well in stews, pasta dishes, or as a filling for pies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags for up to 3 months. Check for signs of spoilage before use.

venison-or-deer-and-noodles-with-cream-o.title: Venison with Noodles in Cream Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Venison is a lean meat from deer, prized for its delicate flavor and high protein content. Combined with noodles and a cream (white) sauce it becomes a hearty dish popular in European and Asian cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Venison contains less fat than beef and a higher level of iron.
Traditionally in Scandinavian countries venison is served with potatoes, but nowadays it is often paired with pasta and a cream sauce.
Wild deer feed on natural vegetation, giving their meat a richer profile of omega‑3 fatty acids.
The noodles can be egg‑based or wheat‑based, depending on regional preference.
Cream sauce is usually made from cream, butter and flour, but it can be replaced with a light white sauce made from stock and milk.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Venison provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with beef, venison has less saturated fat, which is beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: High iron content
items.content: The iron in venison is highly bioavailable and helps maintain healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Venison supplies B12, B6 and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Provides zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals support immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to game meat.

items.title: Parasite risk
items.content: Raw or undercooked venison can harbor parasites; ensure thorough cooking.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: People with gout should limit venison intake.

items.title: Sodium in sauce
items.content: Prepared cream sauces often contain a lot of salt; control the amount used.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the venison into thin strips, quickly sear, then add to boiled noodles and cream sauce. Garnish with fresh herbs, mushrooms or fried onions.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh venison in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C for up to 2 days or freeze at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Cooked dish should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days.
